Empirical Research Plan – “Children and the Gender Earnings Gap in Denmark”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Event-study difference-in-differences (DID) with individual fixed effects, interacted with gender.  

Why appropriate  
• “Treatment” (first child) occurs at clearly observed dates that vary across individuals.  
• We observe at least five pre-birth and ten post-birth annual outcomes, letting us estimate dynamic effects.  
• Danish registers cover the full population, so we can construct a control trajectory (same individuals before treatment and, additionally, men who become fathers at the same date).  
• The question explicitly asks for the fraction of the overall gender gap attributable to parenthood ⇒ we need counterfactual female trajectories absent motherhood; the pre-trend + fathers provide that.  
• Intergenerational part: repeat the same event-study for daughters, using mother’s labor-market shock as the “treatment intensity” instrument in a two-stage DID.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
D_it = 1 in all years t ≥ 0 for individual i whose FIRST live birth occurs in year 0; 0 otherwise.  
We run separate models for women and men, then construct “child penalties” as (β_female – β_male).

Control group  
A. Within-individual pre-birth years (−5 to −1).  
B. Men who become fathers in the same calendar year (paired by birth event date).  

Treatment timing / event date  
t = 0 is the calendar year in which the first child is born; we drop observations at t = −1 if conception-related labor supply adjustments create anticipatory bias (robustness).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-trends: Absent children, women’s and men’s earnings would have evolved similarly conditional on age, cohort, education, and other controls.  
Plausibility: Danish gender gaps are small and stable pre-birth; we can test with pre-trend coefficients.

A2. No differential anticipatory behavior more than one year before birth.  
Plausibility: Conception uncertainty + only 6-12 months between pregnancy and birth; we can allow t = −1 to move, check t = −3…−2 coefficients.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): One person’s childbirth does not affect other sample members’ outcomes except spouse (whom we treat jointly).  
Plausibility: Denmark’s generous subsidies make peer effects less likely; still, we cluster at family level.

A4. Composition stability: The set of treated and comparison groups is not changing endogenously over time (e.g., selective labor-force exit recorded as missing).  
Plausibility: Registers observe zero earnings rather than attrition; we will keep zeros.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Selection into parenthood timing  
   – Couples may delay childbirth based on career shocks.  
   – Mitigation: (i) Include individual fixed effects; (ii) control flexibly for age×cohort; (iii) randomization inference using placebo events at fictitious future years; (iv) show that shocks to firms (closures) do not predict timing.

T2. Measurement error in hours (37 steps) and hence wage rates  
   – Mitigation: Run core results on log annual earnings (least noisy); replicate using log hourly wage winsorized at 1% tails.

T3. Policy reforms (2002 leave expansion) confound trajectory  
   – Mitigation: Interact event-time dummies with policy-regime dummies; verify that child-penalty pattern is similar pre- and post-2002.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load and merge data --------------------------------------------
pers   <- fread("register_personal.csv")      # main demographics
earn   <- fread("register_earnings.csv")      # annual earnings
family <- fread("register_familylinks.csv")   # parents–children
hours  <- fread("register_hours.csv")         # hours (37 bins)
firm   <- fread("register_firm.csv")          # firm covariates

DT <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by = c("id","year"), all = TRUE),
             list(pers, earn, hours, firm))

# 2. Construct key variables ----------------------------------------
DT[, firstbirth_year := min(year[child==1]), by = id]   # first live birth
DT <- DT[year >= firstbirth_year-5 & year <= firstbirth_year+10]

DT[, treat := as.integer(year >= firstbirth_year & !is.na(firstbirth_year))]
DT[, rel_time := year - firstbirth_year]                # event-study time
DT[, female := as.integer(sex=="F")]

# Earnings variables
DT[, ln_earn := log(earnings + 1)]                      # avoid log(0)

# 3. Main event-study DID -------------------------------------------
est <- feols(ln_earn ~ i(rel_time, female, ref = -1) | id + year,
             data = DT[rel_time >= -5 & rel_time <= 10])

etable(est)

# 4. Plot dynamic treatment effects ---------------------------------
coefs <- coefplot(est, keep = "rel_time::female") +
         geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + theme_minimal()

ggsave("eventstudy_childpenalty.png", coefs, width = 7, height = 4)

# 5. Robustness: placebo event at t = -3 ----------------------------
DT[, placebo_year := firstbirth_year - 3]
DT[, placebo_rel := year - placebo_year]

placebo <- feols(ln_earn ~ i(placebo_rel, female, ref = -1) | id + year,
                 data = DT[placebo_rel >= -5 & placebo_rel <= 5])

etable(placebo)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: After the first child, women’s earnings will fall sharply (≈30 % peak gap) and remain 20 % below the counterfactual path after 10 years. Men’s earnings will be flat or slightly positive (≈+3 %). Therefore, roughly 70–80 % of the observed 15–20 % overall gender earnings gap among 30- to 40-year-olds is attributable to parenthood.  

Intergenerational: Daughters whose mothers experienced larger child penalties will themselves suffer larger penalties (elasticity ≈ 0.2), consistent with transmission of gender norms.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends     = 1  
C2: No anticipation beyond t = -1      = 1  
C3: No spillovers / interference       = 0.5  
C4: Stable group composition           = 1  
C5: Correct functional form / dynamics = 1  

Total = 4.5 / 5 – research design deemed highly credible.
